editorialNote: Additive research batch on Southeast Asian polities, maritime networks and Pacific settlement and navigation. Entries are research-enriched and remain pending independent editorial review. References provide traceability and further reading; they do not certify every claim.

nodes.title: Srivijaya
nodes.short: A maritime Buddhist polity based in Sumatra that linked ports across the Strait of Malacca and wider Asian trade routes.
nodes.description: Srivijaya was a maritime polity centred around southern Sumatra, with Palembang often identified as an important early centre. Its influence grew through control of strategic sea passages, port networks and relationships with merchants and Buddhist institutions. Its reach and political structure changed over time, and historians reconstruct its history from inscriptions, archaeology and external records.

nodes.title: Majapahit Empire
nodes.short: A Javanese kingdom whose court, commerce and literary culture shaped a major period in Indonesian history.
nodes.description: Majapahit emerged in eastern Java in the late thirteenth century and became a major political and cultural power in the Indonesian archipelago. Its influence depended on a combination of court authority, alliances, trade and regional relationships; the extent of direct control beyond Java remains debated. The court's literary and artistic legacy is an important source for understanding the period.

nodes.title: Khmer Empire
nodes.short: A mainland Southeast Asian empire whose capitals and monuments transformed the landscape around Angkor.
nodes.description: The Khmer Empire developed around the Tonle Sap and Mekong region, with Angkor serving as a major political and ceremonial centre for much of its history. Its rulers sponsored extensive temple construction, urban works and water-management infrastructure. The empire interacted with neighbouring societies through diplomacy, warfare, religious exchange and commerce; its history cannot be reduced to the monuments alone.

nodes.title: Angkorian Water Management
nodes.short: A landscape-scale system of reservoirs, canals, embankments and waterways that supported the Angkor region.
nodes.description: The Angkor region contains an extensive network of reservoirs, canals, embankments and other hydraulic features. These works helped manage water in a monsoonal environment and were connected to agriculture, settlement, transport and political authority. Archaeologists continue to debate how the system functioned in different periods, so it should not be described as one unchanged master plan.

nodes.title: Champa
nodes.short: A succession of Cham polities along the coast of central and southern Vietnam, connected to regional maritime trade.
nodes.description: Champa refers to a changing set of Cham political centres along the coast of present-day central and southern Vietnam. Chinese records mention Cham polities from the early centuries CE, while inscriptions, temples, ceramics and other archaeological evidence illuminate their history. Cham communities participated in maritime exchange across the South China Sea and retain a distinct cultural presence today.

nodes.title: Funan
nodes.short: An early Mekong-region polity known through archaeology and accounts preserved in Chinese historical texts.
nodes.description: Funan is the name used in Chinese sources for an early political and commercial formation in the lower Mekong region. Archaeological evidence, including the port settlement of Óc Eo, points to connections among local communities and traders from South and East Asia. The precise boundaries, political organisation and relationship between Funan and later states remain subjects of scholarly debate.

nodes.title: Bagan Civilisation
nodes.short: A major centre of Buddhist art, architecture and political power on the Ayeyarwady River in present-day Myanmar.
nodes.description: Bagan became the centre of a powerful kingdom in the central plains of present-day Myanmar. Between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries, rulers and donors supported the construction of thousands of Buddhist monuments, creating a distinctive sacred landscape. River transport, agricultural resources, religious patronage and regional networks all contributed to Bagan's importance.

nodes.title: Ayutthaya Kingdom
nodes.short: A Siamese kingdom whose riverine capital became a major centre of diplomacy and international commerce.
nodes.description: The Ayutthaya Kingdom was founded in the mid-fourteenth century and developed a capital on an island formed by rivers in central Thailand. Its location supported trade, transport and defence, and the city became a cosmopolitan centre visited by merchants and diplomatic missions. Burmese forces destroyed the capital in 1767, leaving an extensive archaeological landscape.

nodes.title: Malacca Sultanate
nodes.short: A Malay sultanate whose port became a pivotal meeting place for merchants across the Indian Ocean and East Asia.
nodes.description: The Malacca Sultanate grew around a strategically placed port on the Strait of Malacca. Its commercial importance rested on maritime routes linking the Indian Ocean and South China Sea, as well as the port's political institutions and trading communities. Portuguese conquest in 1511 changed the region's political order, but Melaka continued to reflect centuries of cultural exchange.

nodes.title: Borobudur Temple
nodes.short: A monumental Buddhist complex in central Java that combines architecture, sculpture and a carefully designed pilgrimage route.
nodes.description: Borobudur was built in central Java during the eighth and ninth centuries under the Sailendra dynasty. Its terraces, narrative reliefs, Buddha images and stupas create an architectural route associated with Buddhist ideas and practice. The monument is also evidence of the artistic and political worlds of early medieval Java and of the long history of conservation in Indonesia.

nodes.title: Sukhothai Kingdom
nodes.short: An early Siamese kingdom associated with distinctive Thai art, inscriptions, Buddhist monuments and water engineering.
nodes.description: Sukhothai was a political and cultural centre in northern-central Thailand during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Its associated towns shared roads, water infrastructure and commercial links, while inscriptions and monuments document developments in language, religion, law and artistic styles. The kingdom's later national significance should be understood alongside the wider and more complex history of the region.

nodes.title: Pyu Ancient Cities
nodes.short: Early urban centres in the Ayeyarwady basin that developed distinctive Buddhist, agricultural and water-management traditions.
nodes.description: Halin, Beikthano and Sri Ksetra were major Pyu urban centres in the dry zone of the Ayeyarwady basin. Their archaeological remains include city walls, stupas, production areas, burial sites and irrigation features. The cities participated in long-distance trade and helped shape the spread of Buddhist institutions and urban forms in mainland Southeast Asia.

nodes.title: Polynesian Wayfinding
nodes.short: A sophisticated body of ocean-navigation knowledge based on stars, winds, swells, currents, birds and environmental observation.
nodes.description: Polynesian wayfinding traditions enabled long-distance voyages across a vast ocean without relying on modern magnetic or satellite instruments. Navigators interpreted star paths, ocean swells, wind patterns, clouds, birds and other signs as parts of an integrated knowledge system. These practices vary across communities and are sustained and renewed through contemporary voyaging and cultural education.

nodes.title: Lapita Cultural Complex
nodes.short: An archaeological tradition recognised through distinctive pottery and settlement evidence across parts of the western and central Pacific.
nodes.description: Lapita is an archaeological complex identified especially through distinctive dentate-stamped pottery and associated settlement remains. Its communities were involved in the movement of people, plants, animals and technologies across Near and Remote Oceania. The origins and development of Lapita are active research topics, and pottery styles should not be treated as a simple label for one uniform people.

nodes.title: Rapa Nui Culture
nodes.short: The living Polynesian culture of Rapa Nui, known internationally for its monumental moai and distinctive island history.
nodes.description: Rapa Nui is the homeland of a Polynesian people whose ancestors settled the remote island in the southeastern Pacific. Its archaeological landscape includes moai statues, ahu ceremonial platforms, settlements, agricultural features and rock art. The island's history also includes severe disruption through colonial intrusion, disease and enslavement, while Rapa Nui people continue to maintain and renew their culture.

nodes.title: Taputapuātea
nodes.short: A major marae complex on Raiatea that symbolises ancestral connections and the shared heritage of Polynesian communities.
nodes.description: Taputapuātea, on the island of Raiatea in French Polynesia, is a ceremonial landscape centred on a marae complex. It is associated with political, religious and social relationships among communities across the wider Polynesian world. The site also reflects voyaging knowledge and the movement of people and cultural practices between islands; it remains important to living communities.

nodes.title: Maritime Southeast Asian Trade Networks
nodes.short: Interconnected sea routes that linked ports in Southeast Asia with South Asia, China, the Middle East and beyond.
nodes.description: Maritime Southeast Asian trade developed through overlapping routes across the Bay of Bengal, Strait of Malacca and South China Sea. Port communities exchanged goods, technologies, religious ideas and artistic forms, while monsoon winds shaped seasonal travel. These networks were not controlled by one empire; their organisation shifted with ports, political alliances and changing demand.

nodes.title: Māori Settlement of Aotearoa
nodes.short: The settlement of Aotearoa by Polynesian voyagers and the development of distinct Māori communities and traditions.
nodes.description: The ancestors of Māori reached Aotearoa New Zealand through deliberate ocean voyages from East Polynesia, with current scholarship commonly placing settlement in the late thirteenth century. The exact routes, dates and number of voyages remain debated. Māori oral traditions, archaeology, language and environmental evidence all contribute to understanding settlement and the formation of distinct iwi and hapū.

claims.claim: Srivijaya's influence depended on maritime routes and port relationships around the Strait of Malacca, rather than on a single continuous land empire.
Inscriptions and external accounts are central to reconstructing Srivijaya, and the location and reach of its political centres changed over time.
Majapahit became a major political power in Java after its establishment in 1293, with its influence extending through changing alliances and maritime relationships.
The extent of Majapahit's authority across the archipelago is debated; claims of uniform territorial control should be treated cautiously.
Angkor was a major political and ceremonial centre within the long history of the Khmer Empire, with monuments and urban remains documenting several phases of development.
Khmer rulers and communities shaped a regional cultural landscape through temple building, water infrastructure and exchanges with neighbouring societies.
Angkor's hydraulic landscape includes reservoirs, canals and embankments that connected water management with settlement and agriculture.
The Angkorian water system changed over time, and current scholarship does not support treating it as one static or perfectly centralised design.
Cham polities along the central Vietnamese coast participated in maritime trade and maintained artistic and political traditions distinct from neighbouring states.
The history of Champa is reconstructed from inscriptions, archaeology and external records, and its political geography changed across many centuries.
Archaeological evidence from sites such as Óc Eo indicates that early Mekong-region communities participated in long-distance exchange linking South and East Asia.
Funan is a historical label derived largely from external texts, so its territorial extent and political organisation remain uncertain.
Bagan became a major centre of Buddhist art and architecture during the eleventh to thirteenth centuries, leaving a large and varied monument landscape.
River transport, religious patronage and regional exchange were important to Bagan's development as a political and sacred centre.
Ayutthaya's riverine location connected its capital to maritime commerce and helped shape its role as a diplomatic and trading centre.
The capital was destroyed in 1767, and its surviving urban layout, temples and waterworks provide evidence for its earlier scale and organisation.
The Malacca port occupied a strategic position on the sea route between the Indian Ocean and South China Sea, attracting merchants from multiple regions.
The later history of Melaka reflects successive Malay, Portuguese, Dutch and other influences arising from centuries of trade and cultural exchange.
Borobudur was built in central Java in the eighth and ninth centuries and combines a monumental stupa with terraces, reliefs and sculptural programmes.
Borobudur's architecture provides evidence of Buddhist practice and the artistic and political culture of early medieval Java.
The historic towns associated with Sukhothai shared roads and water infrastructure that linked political, religious and commercial functions.
Sukhothai's monuments and inscriptions document an important period in the development of Siamese art, writing and political institutions.
The Pyu cities combined walled urban layouts, Buddhist monuments, production sites and irrigation features in the Ayeyarwady basin.
Archaeological evidence from the Pyu cities documents long-distance trade and early Buddhist urban communities in mainland Southeast Asia.
Polynesian navigators used integrated observations of stars, winds, swells, currents, clouds and wildlife to travel across the Pacific.
Wayfinding is a living knowledge tradition that is being taught and practised in contemporary voyaging, not merely a technique preserved in the distant past.
Lapita is identified archaeologically through distinctive pottery and settlement evidence distributed across parts of the western and central Pacific.
The origins and cultural relationships of Lapita communities remain subjects of research, and the archaeological label should not be equated with a single homogeneous ethnic group.
Rapa Nui's archaeological landscape includes moai, ahu, settlements and evidence of agricultural and ceremonial activity.
The history of Rapa Nui includes the enduring cultural life of its people as well as severe disruption from colonial intrusion, disease and enslavement.
Taputapuātea is a marae complex that expresses social, religious and ancestral relationships within the wider Polynesian world.
The site's cultural significance includes voyaging knowledge and living connections among communities across the Pacific.
Sea routes through the Strait of Malacca and South China Sea linked Southeast Asian ports with wider Indian Ocean and East Asian commercial systems.
Monsoon patterns shaped the timing and direction of maritime travel, while ports and political relationships changed the structure of exchange over time.
Current historical and archaeological scholarship places the settlement of Aotearoa by Polynesian ancestors in the late thirteenth century, while exact dates and routes remain debated.
Māori histories are informed by oral traditions, archaeology, language and environmental evidence, and should not be reduced to a single written account.
